extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical geometry; readers of Archimedes; advanced undergraduate/graduate mathematics/history of mathematics readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the propositions, constructions, and geometric facts about sections, tangents, volumes, and ratios for conoids, spheroids, cones, cylinders, and related solids as given in Archimedes' On Conoids and Spheroids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8 — ellipse is a section of a cone
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse produced by revolution/construction, every point P on the ellipse lies on the surface of some cone so described; hence the ellipse is a section of the cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: drop perpendicularly and use parallels (PN perpendicular to AA', ON produced to meet AD in AM, through M draw HK parallel to A'A', draw MQ perpendicular to plane). Uses equalities of squared segments and parallelism to show PQ is a generator through both Q and P. Proof shows every point of ellipse lies on cone surface; similar argument for all points on ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9 — cylinder through an ellipse with given axis OC
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse and a plane through one axis perpendicular to the plane of the ellipse, and a straight line OC drawn from the centre O in that plane (through the axis but not perpendicular), it is possible to find a cylinder with axis OC such that the ellipse is a section of the cylinder (i.e., circular sections of the cylinder with axis OC pass through the circumference of the given ellipse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw AD, A'E parallel to CO and DE through O perpendicular to AD and A'E. Three cases depending on BB' relative to DE: (1) BB' = DE: describe a circle on DE as diameter in a plane perpendicular to OC and make cylinder with axis OC; show any P on ellipse corresponds to a generator of that cylinder. (2) BB' > DE: take E' on A'E with DE' = BB' and proceed as in (1). (3) BB' < DE: choose K on CO produced such that DO^2 — CB^2 = OR'^2, construct KR perpendicular to paper equal to CB, describe circle on DE as diameter passing through O and draw cylinder; prove any P on ellipse lies on cylinder. Proofs use perpendiculars, parallels, equalities of squared segments (e.g., PN^2 = DM·ME = QM^2) and parallelism of PQ to CO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10 — ratio of cones and segments of cones; cylinder/cone volume relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two cones have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their bases and of their heights. The same method shows that any segments (frusta) of cones have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their bases and of their heights. Also: a frustum of a cylinder is triple of the conical segment which has the same base and equal height; and (cylinder is triple of cone with same base and equal height) follows similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Euclid XII.11 and 14. Notes historical attribution (Eudoxus). These are foundational proportionality/volume relations used later in segment-volume comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11 — sections of solids of revolution are conics or circles
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Paraboloid of revolution: section by a plane through or parallel to the axis is a parabola equal to the generating parabola; axis of section is intersection of cutting plane with plane through axis at right angles to cutting plane. If cut by plane at right angles to axis, section is a circle centred on axis. (2) Hyperboloid of revolution: plane through axis, parallel to axis, or through centre gives hyperbola; if through axes equal to generating hyperbola, if parallel to axes similar, if through centre not similar. Plane at right angles to axis gives circle centred on axis. (3) Spheroidal figures: plane through axis or parallel gives ellipse (equal if through axis, similar if parallel); axis of section is intersection as before. Plane at right angles to axis gives a circle centred on axis. (4) For any of these figures, if a plane through the axis is cut and from any surface point (not on the section) a perpendicular to the plane is drawn, that perpendicular falls within the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes states proofs are evident; these are reductions to plane conic properties and to producing circular sections via planes perpendicular to axis. The statement enumerates cases and clarifies where centres/axes lie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12 — oblique section of paraboloid is ellipse with specified axes
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paraboloid of revolution is cut by a plane neither parallel nor perpendicular to the axis, and if the plane through the axis perpendicular to the cutting plane intersects it in a segment RR' (the portion inside the paraboloid), the section is an ellipse whose major axis is RR' and whose minor axis equals the perpendicular distance between the lines through R and R' parallel to the paraboloid axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set cutting plane perpendicular to paper; construct QM perpendicular to RR' where Q is any point on section and M meets plane through axis. Use circular section in plane through DMFE perpendicular to axis: QM^2 = DM·ME. Relate tangents and similar triangles to show locus of Q is an ellipse with major axis RR' and minor axis equal to R'H. Proof uses properties of parabolic tangents (Prop.3) and similar triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 13–14 — oblique sections of hyperboloid/spheroid that meet all generators are ellipses with major axis RR'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hyperboloid of revolution is cut by a plane meeting all the generators of the enveloping cone, or if an 'oblong' spheroid is cut by a plane not perpendicular to the axis, and if a plane through the axis intersects the cutting plane at right angles in a straight line where the hyperboloid or spheroid intercepts length RR', then the section by the cutting plane is an ellipse whose major axis is RR'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument parallels Proposition 12: take point Q on section, draw QM ⟂ RR', form plane perpendicular to axis cutting figure in a circle so QM^2 = DM·ME; use tangent PT parallel to RR' and properties of hyperbola/ellipse to show OA < OP (or OA <?) and thereby that the locus is an ellipse with major axis RR'. Corollaries: for flat spheroid RR' may be minor axis; parallel sections are similar because OA^2:OP^2 constant for parallel sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 — lines from surface parallel to axis / tangent plane uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) From any point on the surface: for paraboloid, a line drawn parallel to axis; for hyperboloid, a line drawn parallel to any line through the vertex of the enveloping cone — the part of that line in the convex direction falls outside the surface, the other part within. (2) If a plane touches a conoid without cutting it, it touches at one point only, and the plane through the point of contact and the axis is perpendicular to the tangent plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to plane sections: draw plane through axis (or through point and given line) to get a conic whose tangency properties give the result. For uniqueness of tangent plane: if touched at two points contradiction follows because line joining points would lie within conoid but also be in tangent plane which does not cut the solid. For perpendicularity of plane through point and axis to tangent plane, argue via circular sections and perpendicular tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 — tangent properties for spheroidal figures
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) If a plane touches any spheroidal figure without cutting it, it touches at one point only and the plane through the point of contact and the axis is at right angles to the tangent plane. (2) If a conoid or spheroid is cut by a plane through the axis, and through any tangent to the resulting conic a plane is erected at right angles to the plane of section, that plane will touch the conoid or spheroid at the same point as the line touches the conic. (3) If two parallel planes touch any spheroidal figure, the line joining the points of contact passes through the centre of the spheroid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce to plane geometry: (2) uses perpendicular construction and Proposition 11(4). For (3) if planes are not perpendicular to axis reduce to plane problem via plane through axis; if they are perpendicular it's obvious. These are general tangent/contact properties linking plane and plane-section tangency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 17 — a parallel plane through centre and chord-of-contact line relation
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel planes touch any spheroidal figures, and another plane is drawn parallel to the tangent planes and passing through the centre, then a line drawn through any point of the circumference of the resulting section parallel to the chord of contact of the tangent planes will fall outside the spheroid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by reduction to plane proposition. Archimedes adds the evident corollary: if the plane parallel to tangent planes does not pass through centre, the corresponding straight line falls without the spheroid in direction of smaller segment but within it in the other direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18 — plane through centre bisects spheroid (surface and volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any spheroidal figure cut by a plane through the centre is divided, both as regards its surface and its volume, into two equal parts by that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses method of application and comparison with another equal and similar spheroid divided similarly; effectively symmetry about centre ensures equal halves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 19–20 — approximation of segments by inscribed/circumscribed cylinder-frusta assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a segment cut off by a plane from a paraboloid or hyperboloid of revolution, or a segment of a spheroid less than half the spheroid, it is possible to inscribe in the segment one solid and circumscribe about it another solid, each made up of cylinders or frusta of cylinders of equal height, such that the circumscribed figure exceeds the inscribed figure by a volume less than that of any given solid (i.e., arbitrary close approximation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take the plane base perpendicular to paper, reduce to plane conic section BAC. Let HAF be tangent parallel to BC and use plane through this tangent to touch solid at A (vertex). Describe cylinder or frustum with axis AD through base circle/ellipse. Divide cylinder/frustum into equal-height parts by planes parallel to base; at each parallel draw corresponding cylinders/frusta forming inscribed and circumscribed approximants. Show successive additions give difference less than any given solid by choosing subdivisions fine enough; use arithmetic progressions and pairwise equalities of corresponding parts to bound differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 21–22 — paraboloid segment volume equals 3/2 of cone (same base and axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any segment of a paraboloid of revolution is half as large again (i.e. 3/2) as the cone or segment of a cone which has the same base and the same axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set base perpendicular to plane of paper, reduce to parabolic section BAC, tangent EF parallel to BC at A. Use cylinder/frustum approximations (Prop.19) and properties of cones vs cylinders (Prop.10) together with arithmetic comparisons of corresponding cylinder/frusta slices to derive contradiction if segment were not 3/2 the cone; hence equality. Proof involves inscribed/circumscribed constructions and combining volume ratios using sequences in arithmetical progression and attendant lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 23 — equality of paraboloid segments with equal axes
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a paraboloid of revolution two segments are cut off, one by a plane perpendicular to the axis and the other by a plane not perpendicular, and if the axes of the segments are equal, the segments will be equal in volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to plane: assume planes perpendicular to paper, axes equal AN and PV. Use equal triangles in parabolic section (Prop.3) and compare cones with same bases and vertices A and P: ratio of cones compounded of base ratios and heights yields equality because of equal axes; since segments are each half as large again as respective cones (Prop.22), segments are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 — paraboloid segments proportional to squares of axes
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a paraboloid of revolution two segments are cut off by planes in any manner, the segments will be to one another as the squares on their axes (i.e., volumes ∝ axis^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct cones with same bases and common vertex A; by Prop.23 segments corresponding to equal axes are equal. Show cones are in ratio AN^2 : AN'^2 by relating cone volumes to base radii/proportions and heights, giving segments in ratio of squares of axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 25–26 — hyperboloid segment to corresponding cone ratio formula
rubrics_metrics.description: In any hyperboloid of revolution, if A is vertex and AD the axis of any segment cut off by a plane, and if CA is the semidiameter through A (on same line as AD), then (segment) : (cone with same base and axis) = (AD + 3·CA) : (AD + 2·CA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set cutting plane perpendicular to paper, take hyperbolic section BAB' with center C (vertex of enveloping cone). Let tangent EF at A be parallel to BB'. Construct cylinder/frustum through base and compare to cones. Use inscribed/circumscribed cylinder-frusta approximations with carefully chosen arithmetic arrangements of component volumes and gnomons, combine via previous propositions and lemmas to derive the ratio, using contradiction argument if not equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 27–29 — spheroid segment ratio formulas and special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) In any spheroid with centre C, if a plane meeting the axis cuts off a segment (≤ half the spheroid) with vertex A and axis AD, and if A'D is axis of remaining segment, then (first seg.) : (cone or seg. of cone with same base and axis) = (CA + A'D) : A'D [= (3CA - AD) : (2CA - AD)] . (2) Particular case: if the plane passes through the centre so segment is half the spheroid, that half-spheroid is double the cone (i.e., half the spheroid = 2 × cone with same vertex and axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: consider elliptic section ABA'B', tangents EF, E'K parallel to BB' touch at A,A'; draw planes through these tangents to touch spheroid. Draw cylinder/frustum through base and compare via inscribed/circumscribed cylinder-frusta arguments as in previous propositions. Use arithmetic decomposition into rectangles/gnomons and application of previous lemmas (Prop.1, Prop.2, Prop.10) to reach the stated proportion; special case where plane through centre yields factor 2 relation.
